clue.text: Front part of animal in square hole, did you say?

indicators.note: asking whether you said something points to what was spoken rather than what is written

blocks.note: a square has four sides, and a pore is a tiny hole in the skin

explanation.surface: Someone describes an animal poking its front end into a square hole, and checks they heard right.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Square' is read loosely as FOUR (a square's sides) and 'hole' as PORE; said in a non-rhotic British accent, 'four pore' matches FOREPAW.
explanation.definitionFit: A forepaw is the paw on a front leg, so it is literally a front part of an animal.

clue.text: Cheese in hamper, we hear?

indicators.note: hearing rather than reading means the word is chosen for its sound

blocks.note: to hamper movement is to fetter it, as with a chain on the leg

explanation.surface: Cheese packed into a picnic hamper.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Hamper' looks like the basket the cheese sits in, but it is the verb meaning restrain; FETTER said in a British accent matches FETA.
explanation.definitionFit: Feta is a white brined Greek cheese made from sheep or goat milk.

clue.text: Violent con mellowing

blocks.note: a ramp is old British slang for a swindle
wine or cheese mellows as it ages

explanation.surface: A violent prisoner is gradually softening with time.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Con' looks like a convict, but here it is a swindle, which British slang calls a RAMP.
explanation.definitionFit: Rampaging means rushing about wildly and destructively, which is violent behaviour.

clue.text: Russian work of art on show?

blocks.note: first meaning: Mussorgsky's suite for piano, later orchestrated by Ravel
second meaning: paintings displayed in a gallery, read literally

explanation.walkthrough: The clue reads as one phrase about a Russian artwork in a gallery; split it and the title of Mussorgsky's suite also describes exactly that.
explanation.definitionFit: The composer Modest Mussorgsky wrote the piece, and literally paintings hung in a gallery are displayed images seen by visitors.

clue.text: One political side has head that’s screwed on

definitions.note: a description of the thing rather than a noun naming it

blocks.note: a party's left or right wing
nut is slang for the head

explanation.surface: A politician of one faction is praised for having their head screwed on, that is, being sensible.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Has your head screwed on' is an idiom for being sensible, which hides that the definition is a part screwed onto a bolt.
explanation.definitionFit: A wing nut is a fastener with two flat projections, turned by hand onto a threaded bolt.

clue.text: Poisonous plant is on description of computer

indicators.note: in an across clue, one thing placed on another comes after it, so the first-named piece goes second

blocks.note: a computer is a digital machine
taken as written

explanation.surface: A toxic plant has been written up in a computer's specification.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Description of computer' asks for an adjective, not a noun: the word that describes how a computer works.
explanation.definitionFit: Digitalis is the foxglove, a garden plant whose leaves are toxic and yield a heart drug.

clue.text: Evidence of bigamy mumbo jumbo?

blocks.note: first meaning, cryptic: Dutch is old rhyming slang for wife, so two of them would be bigamy
second meaning: unintelligible talk, gibberish

explanation.walkthrough: 'My old Dutch' is Cockney slang for a wife (short for duchess), so a double one means two wives at once.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrase is an everyday idiom for incomprehensible language, just as mumbo jumbo means meaningless gibberish.

clue.text: Monochrome artwork is article obscured by screen

indicators.note: whatever is obscured is hidden behind or within something else, so one piece goes inside another

blocks.note: a grille is a grating that screens an opening
taken as written
the indefinite article

explanation.surface: A black-and-white artwork has an item hidden behind a screen.
explanation.walkthrough: IS and A go together into the grille, between its R and I.
explanation.definitionFit: Grisaille is a painting technique done entirely in shades of grey, giving a monochrome image.

clue.text: Leader in Augustus wearing clothes — these?

definitions.text: Leader in Augustus wearing clothes — these?

indicators.note: the leader of a word is the letter at its front
to wear something is to have it around you, so one piece goes inside another

blocks.note: the opening letter of the emperor's name
togs is informal British for clothes

explanation.surface: The Roman emperor is pictured in his robes, and the clue asks what they were.
explanation.walkthrough: The whole clue is both wordplay and definition: an emperor such as Augustus would wear these garments.
explanation.definitionFit: Togas were the draped woollen robes worn by Roman citizens, the garments an emperor like Augustus wore.

clue.text: Make an effort, as umpire will on dismissal?

blocks.note: first meaning: the idiom for making even a tiny effort
second meaning, cryptic: a cricket umpire raises an index finger to give a batsman out

explanation.walkthrough: In cricket a batsman is given out when the umpire raises one finger, so the literal action is what the official does on a dismissal.
explanation.definitionFit: The idiom, usually in the negative, means to do the least bit of work or exert yourself at all.

clue.text: Ice hardened, sphere enclosed

indicators.note: something enclosed is shut inside something else

blocks.note: jelly or concrete sets when it hardens
an orb is a sphere

explanation.surface: Water froze around a ball trapped inside it.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Ice' looks like a subject frozen hard, but it is the dessert sense of a water ice.
explanation.definitionFit: A sorbet is a frozen dessert of sweetened fruit juice, known in Britain as a water ice.

clue.text: Weary flyer

blocks.note: first meaning: to tire or lose energy
second meaning: a banner that flies from a pole

explanation.walkthrough: The pair suggests a tired bird or pilot; 'flyer' is anything that flies, here a banner on a mast.
explanation.definitionFit: Runners flag when they tire, and a flag is a cloth that flutters and flies from a mast.

clue.text: Places to go, see, more or less

blocks.note: loo is British for toilet, a place you go when you need to go
a see is a bishop's diocese, and Ely is one in Cambridgeshire

explanation.surface: A traveller lists places to go and things to see, roughly.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Places to go, see' reads like tourist advice, but 'go' is the toilet euphemism and 'see' is a bishop's seat.
explanation.definitionFit: Speaking loosely means approximately rather than precisely, which is what more or less conveys.

clue.text: Winner in the end, champ hugged by haggard relative

indicators.note: the end of a word is its final letter
to be hugged is to be held within arms, so one piece sits inside another

blocks.note: a gaunt face is haggard and drawn
the closing letter of the word
to champ is to chew noisily, that is to eat

explanation.surface: An elderly, worn-looking relative embraces the victorious champion.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Champ' looks like short for champion, but it is the verb meaning chew noisily, as a horse champs at the bit.
explanation.definitionFit: A great-aunt is a parent's aunt, a member of the family two generations up.

clue.text: Promptly ignored, as bullet passing through brain?

annotation.answer: IN ONE EAR AND OUT THE OTHER

blocks.note: first meaning: said of advice heard and instantly forgotten
second meaning, cryptic: the literal path of a shot through the head

explanation.walkthrough: The idiom normally describes words that make no impression; read literally it is the grisly route of a bullet straight through the skull.
explanation.definitionFit: The idiom describes instructions heard and immediately forgotten, so they are disregarded almost at once.

clue.text: Laborious, as is sentiment, for example?

blocks.note: first meaning: taking a long time to do
second meaning, cryptic: the word 'sentiment' has the word for duration inside it, swallowing it up

explanation.walkthrough: Read literally, the hyphenated answer means 'eating up time', and SEN-TIME-NT does exactly that to the four-letter word in its middle.
explanation.definitionFit: A laborious job takes up many hours, so it is slow and demanding work.

clue.text: Dance a good way with expression of support

blocks.note: going a good way is going far
and joins things together, as with does
the Spanish cheer of approval

explanation.surface: Dancing is a good way to go, and the crowd cheers it on.
explanation.walkthrough: 'With' looks like a link but supplies letters itself, the common swap of 'with' for AND.
explanation.definitionFit: A farandole is a lively Provençal folk dance in which a chain of people wind through the streets.

clue.text: Riotous antics from Australian savage

indicators.note: savage treatment mauls and tears apart, so the letters are torn up and rebuilt

blocks.note: the letters as printed

explanation.surface: Wild behaviour comes from a fierce Australian.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Savage' reads as an adjective describing the Australian; it is the signal to mangle the word.
explanation.definitionFit: The Saturnalia was a Roman winter festival of unrestrained revelry, so the word now means wild, riotous merrymaking.

clue.text: Crawling bug silences cat that’s skittish

indicators.note: a skittish animal jumps about unpredictably, so the letters are jumbled

blocks.note: the letters as printed

explanation.surface: A creepy-crawly makes a nervous cat freeze in silence.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Silences' reads as a verb with 'bug' its subject; in fact 'Crawling bug' is the definition and the next two words are the raw letters.
explanation.definitionFit: Scale insects are small sap-sucking bugs; young ones crawl about before settling under a protective waxy shell.

clue.text: Possibly West banks in US state

indicators.note: river banks lie on both sides of the water, so one piece flanks another

blocks.note: Mae West, the Hollywood actress, is one possible West
taken as written

explanation.surface: Perhaps somebody called West puts money into a bank in an American state.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Banks' looks like a noun or a money verb; it means flanks, and 'Possibly' warns that West is just one example of a name.
explanation.definitionFit: Maine is the north-eastern state of the USA, bordering Canada and the Atlantic coast.

clue.text: Third note planned includes first two in diagram

indicators.note: the opening pair of letters of a word is taken
to include something is to take it inside, so one piece goes within another

blocks.note: what you planned is what you meant to do
the opening pair of the word

explanation.surface: A musician's planned score includes a diagram, with a note on the third degree.
explanation.walkthrough: 'In' here only links the selection to its source word.
explanation.definitionFit: In music theory the mediant is the third degree of a major or minor scale, halfway between tonic and dominant.

clue.text: Island a bit windy, dock accessed via gates

indicators.note: something windy is blown about, so the letters are scattered and rebuilt

blocks.note: the letters as printed

explanation.surface: A breezy island has a harbour entered through lock gates.
explanation.walkthrough: 'A bit windy' reads as mild weather; 'a bit' belongs to the letters and only 'windy' is the signal.
explanation.definitionFit: A tidal basin is an enclosed harbour basin whose water level is held by gates against the rise and fall of the tide.

clue.text: All going one way, leading another way

indicators.note: arranged another way means the letters are put in a different order

blocks.note: the letters as printed

explanation.surface: Everyone heads in the same direction, though the leader takes a different route.
explanation.walkthrough: The repeated 'way' makes the clue sound like directions; the second one is the signal to rearrange.
explanation.definitionFit: Things that are aligned are lined up in the same direction, so they all point or travel together.

clue.text: Good day with copper in conversation?

indicators.note: conversation is spoken, so the letters are heard rather than read

blocks.note: Cu is the chemical symbol for copper, spoken as its two letters

explanation.surface: Someone chats with a police officer and wishes them a good day.

explanation.definitionFit: Good day can be said on leaving, a parting phrase just like the casual farewell meaning goodbye.

clue.text: Top location of Welsh castle

blocks.note: first meaning: a knitted jacket buttoned at the front
second meaning: a coastal town in west Wales with a castle

explanation.walkthrough: 'Top' looks like it means summit, which fits a castle; it is a garment.
explanation.definitionFit: A top is any upper-body garment, and a cardigan is a buttoned knitted one; the Welsh town has a Norman castle.

clue.text: Setter for example is encapsulated by “drab, opinionated type”

indicators.note: something encapsulated is sealed inside a capsule, so one piece sits within another

blocks.note: a setter is a breed of gundog
a matt surface is dull and drab
taken as written

explanation.surface: A crossword setter is pigeonholed in a quotation as dull and bigoted.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Setter' invites thoughts of the crossword compiler, but 'for example' marks it as one type of dog.
explanation.definitionFit: A dogmatist asserts beliefs as unquestionable truth, which is exactly an opinionated person.

clue.text: Business in ashes, refinery vacated

indicators.note: a vacated building is emptied, so only the outer letters of the word remain

blocks.note: taken as written
ashes and dust are the remains after burning
just its first and last letters

explanation.surface: A firm lies in ruins after its refinery burns down and is abandoned.
explanation.walkthrough: The picture of a fire-gutted refinery hides that 'vacated' means emptied of its middle letters.
explanation.definitionFit: Industry means commercial activity or a sector of trade, as in the oil industry, a broad synonym for business.

clue.text: Looking at money in gold boxes

blocks.note: read straight through, across the word breaks

clue.text: Interest rate initially intolerable coming off tracker — might one be in a jam?

definitions.text: might one be in a jam?

indicators.note: initially means at the start, so the opening letter of each of the following words is kept

blocks.note: annual percentage rate, the standard abbreviation for a loan's interest rate
the opening letters of these four words

explanation.surface: A borrower's rate becomes unbearable when a tracker mortgage ends, leaving them in a jam.

explanation.definitionFit: Apricot jam is a common preserve, so the fruit is one thing found in a jam, a pun on being in trouble.

clue.text: Attempt joke

blocks.note: first meaning: a go
second meaning: a wisecrack

explanation.walkthrough: The two words read as a request to try a joke; each is a separate meaning of one noun.
explanation.definitionFit: To have a crack at something is to try it, and a crack is also a quick witty remark.

clue.text: Play damn trash unfortunately, title withdrawn

blocks.note: the letters as printed
a title is a name

explanation.definitionFit: Arms and the Man is an 1894 comedy by George Bernard Shaw satirising romantic ideas of war.

clue.text: Appearing in gloom, unromantic peak in Scotland

indicators.note: something appearing in a phrase is found within it, so the letters are hidden there

blocks.note: read across the comma

explanation.surface: A Scottish mountain looms in the gloom, hardly a romantic sight.
explanation.walkthrough: A Munro is any Scottish mountain over 3,000 feet, named after Sir Hugh Munro who listed them.
explanation.definitionFit: Hillwalkers 'bag' Munros, the Scottish mountains above three thousand feet in height.

clue.text: Outfit exposing much flesh, knight say with blood on one

blocks.note: a knight is one of the men, or pieces, in chess
blood relations are kin
the Roman numeral for one

explanation.surface: A knight in a revealing outfit is splashed with blood.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Knight say' points to a chess piece; 'blood' means family, not gore.
explanation.definitionFit: A mankini is a skimpy one-piece male swimsuit, made famous by the film Borat, that leaves most skin bare.

clue.text: Dull in colour, worker surplus to requirements

indicators.note: in places one thing inside another

blocks.note: dun is a dull greyish-brown
red is a colour
the worker ant

explanation.surface: A worker in drab clothes is laid off as no longer needed.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Dull in colour' reads as one description; split it and it is one colour placed inside another.
explanation.definitionFit: Something redundant is no longer needed, and in Britain a worker made redundant has lost their job.

clue.text: Unknown number defended by God test one’s patience

indicators.note: whatever is defended is surrounded by its protector, so one piece is placed inside

blocks.note: Triton, the Greek sea god, son of Poseidon
algebra uses x, y and z for unknowns

clue.text: Two types of note heard where country music popular?

clue.text: Outstanding save with one leg on a line

taken as written
the abbreviation for line

clue.text: One of those working on oilfield, sycophantic fool?

explanation.walkthrough: 'Those working' suggests oil workers; the first definition is a machine, named for its nodding head.
explanation.definitionFit: The pump's rocking head resembles a donkey nodding, and a fawning idiot is a donkey who just keeps agreeing.

clue.text: Genuinely irritated if I had to go without nicotine, initially

initially means at the start, so only the opening letter is kept

the opening letter

clue.text: Native after small shroud?

explanation.walkthrough: 'Native' is the adjective sense of mother, as in mother tongue meaning native language.

clue.text: Relax with bear on a picnic!

clue.text: Mount in foreign region, did you say?

blocks.note: a clime is a region, usually a distant one with its own climate

explanation.walkthrough: 'Mount' looks like a noun for a mountain; it is the verb, to go up.

clue.text: Become rotten, as chopped vegetables etc may have?

clue.text: China in place, or plastic

clue.text: Speech embraced by a British naval commander?

clue.text: Lion heading for nervous bird

clue.text: Order learned with protest

clue.text: American jerk

blocks.note: first meaning: informal British term for a person from the USA
second meaning: a sudden sharp pull

explanation.walkthrough: The pair reads as an insult aimed at an American; 'jerk' is the verb meaning tug.
explanation.definitionFit: Yank is informal for a US citizen, and to yank is to pull sharply with a jerk.

clue.text: Cutting item first removed from entire satirical magazine

indicators.note: having its first removed means the opening letter is dropped

blocks.note: whole means entire
Punch was a long-running British humour and satire magazine

explanation.surface: A cutting article is pulled from an entire satirical magazine.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Cutting item' reads like a sharply critical piece in a magazine; it is the stationery tool that cuts holes.
explanation.definitionFit: A hole punch is an office device that cuts holes in paper so it can be filed in a binder.

clue.text: Spouse and little kids reportedly in underwear

indicators.note: something reported is passed on by word of mouth, so the sound counts

blocks.note: a spouse may be a wife, and runts are the smallest young

explanation.surface: A wife and the small children are dressed in their underwear.
explanation.walkthrough: Spoken together, wife-runts slides into the brand of men's briefs. Y-fronts are British men's briefs with an inverted-Y seam at the front.
explanation.definitionFit: Y-fronts are men's briefs named after the Y-shaped seam on the front, an item of underwear.
